# One Truth, Three Audiences

Source: https://lowob.com/research/one-truth-three-audiences/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-02-06 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Write one product truth, then one belief statement per audience, then a claims register that says what you can prove. The deck, the homepage and community announcements are all derived from those three. The register is also where regulated and AI claims are checked before they ship.

Write one product truth, then one belief statement per audience, then a claims register that says what you can prove. Everything else (the deck, the homepage, the community announcements) is derived from those three. The product truth is one sentence: what it is, who buys it, and what changed that makes it necessary now. The claims register is a short table of every public claim with its evidence and approver; regulators in the US and UK already expect that evidence to exist before the claim is made.

## The product truth

One sentence with three parts: what it is, who buys it, and what changed that makes it necessary now.

Bad: *"The intelligence layer for the future of work."* No buyer, no reason, no thing.

Better: *"An AI agent that answers support tickets inside the help desk your team already uses, for B2B software companies whose ticket volume grew faster than their headcount."*

The second one is less exciting and much more useful. An investor can size it. A customer can recognise themselves in it. A community member can explain it to a friend.

Each of the three parts does a specific job. "What it is" places the product in a frame the reader already understands. April Dunford, whose positioning method is widely used in B2B software, describes the job of a market category as taking a prospect who knows little about the product and pointing them towards its differentiated value. She adds that a category "doesn't replace your messaging or your sales pitch", and that choosing the category first is "the tail wagging the dog". "Who buys it" stops the sentence from serving everyone. "Why now" is the trend that makes the problem urgent; Dunford treats relevant trends as a layer on top of a clear category, not a substitute for one. The full method sits in our piece on [positioning for complex markets](https://lowob.com/research/positioning-for-complex-markets/).

## One belief per audience

Each audience needs to hold a different belief before it acts. Write them down.

| Audience | Must believe | Proof that works | Proof that doesn't |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Investors | This can be large, this team will win it, and now is the moment | Named customers, usage curves, a credible path to the next milestone | TAM slides, "the future of…" |
| Community | Being here early is worth something real | Access, a role, recognition, a visible say in what ships | Vague token hints, giveaways |
| Customers | It solves my problem, it's safe, and someone like me already uses it | A case study from a peer, an audit, a pilot with clear terms | Your raise, your investors' logos |

The right-hand column matters. Founders reuse proof across audiences because it's what they have. Investor logos impress investors and mean almost nothing to a treasury manager deciding where to deposit.

The investor row reflects how VCs say they decide. In a survey of almost 900 venture capitalists, Gompers and colleagues found 95% of firms named the team as important and 47% named it the single most important factor, with the business model named by 83%. Named customers and usage curves are how a team shows the business model works.

The customer row is often several audiences in one. Forrester's State of Business Buying 2024 found an average of 13 people involved in a purchase decision, and 89% of purchases involving two or more departments. The treasury manager, the finance director and the security reviewer each need a version of the customer belief. They should all trace back to the same truth, which is why the truth is written first. Our explainer on [the buying committee](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-buying-committee/) covers the roles.

When the truth is not written down, it drifts. Gartner's survey of 632 B2B buyers, published in June 2025, found 69% reported inconsistencies between a supplier's website and what its sellers told them. That figure is about sellers and websites, but the same drift happens between a deck, a community channel and a homepage.

> Investor logos impress investors and mean almost nothing to a treasury manager deciding where to deposit.

## The claims register

A short table of every claim you make publicly, with the evidence for each and who approved it. It sounds like compliance. It's actually the fastest way to stop a team saying five different things.

| Claim | Where it appears | Evidence | Evidence date | Approved by | Review date |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The exact wording, as published | Deck, homepage, community post, ad | The test, audit, contract or dataset behind it | When the evidence was produced | One named person | When it must be rechecked |

The register is not a new idea dressed up. The US Federal Trade Commission's Policy Statement Regarding Advertising Substantiation, issued in 1984, requires advertisers to have a "reasonable basis" for objective claims before they are disseminated. Where an advert states a level of support, such as "tests prove", the FTC expects the firm to have at least that level of substantiation. A claims register is simply where that basis is written down.

In Web3 it does double duty: claims about yield, safety and returns carry real regulatory and reputational risk, and the register is where you catch "guaranteed" before it ships. The UK Financial Conduct Authority's regime for cryptoasset promotions has applied since 8 October 2023 to every firm marketing cryptoassets to UK consumers, including firms based overseas. Promotions must be fair, clear and not misleading, carry prescribed risk warnings, and sit inside consumer journeys with positive frictions such as a 24-hour cooling-off period.

In AI it catches the accuracy number that was true on one benchmark in March. In September 2024 the FTC announced Operation AI Comply, five enforcement actions against companies making deceptive AI claims. One concerned a service marketed as "the world's first robot lawyer"; the FTC said the company had not tested its chatbot against human lawyers. The FTC chair at the time said there was "no AI exemption from the laws on the books."

## Where Web3 and AI differ

**Web3:** the token collapses audiences. Your holder is an investor, a community member and sometimes a customer. That makes the product truth more important, not less, because the token story will drown it unless it's written down first. Lead with what the protocol does for a user, and let the token be the mechanism, not the headline. [The user story before the token story](https://lowob.com/research/the-user-story-before-the-token-story/) takes this further.

**AI:** the model is not the product. Investors may care about the model; customers care about the workflow. Position on the job done and the result, and keep the model story for the deck appendix. Our piece [The model is not the product](https://lowob.com/research/the-model-is-not-the-product/) sets out why.

|  | Web3 | AI |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What collapses or splits | Audiences collapse into the token holder | The investor story and the customer story split |
| Lead the truth with | What the protocol does for a user | The workflow and the result |
| Riskiest claims | Yield, safety, returns | Accuracy, autonomy, replacement of a professional |
| Register catches | "Guaranteed" before it ships | The benchmark number that was true once |

Illustrative example: a register catching a claim

Decision
:   Remove an accuracy percentage from the homepage hero and replace it with a named customer's measured result.

Reason and owner
:   The claims register showed the percentage came from a single internal benchmark run six months earlier, with no customer data behind it. Owned by the head of product, approved by the CEO.

What changed
:   The homepage led with a peer result a buyer could check, and the accuracy figure moved to a dated technical note with its method stated.

Illustrative: a composite of an early-stage AI software company, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Write the truth first.** One sentence: what it is, who buys it, and what changed that makes it necessary now.
- **Map proof to belief.** Each audience accepts different proof; investor logos do not persuade a treasury manager.
- **Keep a claims register.** Every public claim, its evidence, its date and its approver, in one table.
- **Let the mechanism follow the use.** In Web3, lead with what the protocol does for a user; in AI, position on the workflow, not the model.

Gateway card

### Before the next deck, homepage or announcement

- A one-sentence product truth: what, who, why now
- A written belief statement for each audience
- The proof each audience will actually accept, mapped
- A claims register with evidence, a date and an owner
- The homepage hero tested on a customer, not an investor

## Common questions

### How do I write a product positioning statement for a startup?

Write one sentence with three parts: what it is, who buys it, and what changed that makes it necessary now. It should be specific enough for an investor to size and a customer to recognise themselves in.

### What is a claims register?

A short table of every claim you make publicly, with the evidence for each, the date of that evidence and who approved it. It stops a team saying different things and catches risky claims about yield, safety or accuracy.

### Do marketing claims legally need evidence?

In the US, the FTC has required a reasonable basis for objective advertising claims since 1984, and applies it to AI claims. In the UK, cryptoasset promotions must be fair, clear and not misleading. Take legal advice for your market.

### What proof do customers want compared with investors?

Investors want named customers, usage curves and a path to the next milestone. Customers want a peer case study, an audit or a pilot with clear terms, not your raise or your investors' logos.

- [April Dunford, Understanding the Job of a Market Category](https://aprildunford.substack.com/p/understanding-the-job-of-a-market), 11 January 2024. Practitioner's newsletter; method, not data.
- [Gompers, Gornall, Kaplan and Strebulaev, How Do Venture Capitalists Make Decisions?](https://corpgov.law.harvard.edu/2019/08/20/how-do-venture-capitalists-make-decisions), Harvard Law School Forum summary, 20 August 2019. Survey of almost 900 VCs; self-reported.
- [Forrester, The State Of Business Buying, 2024](https://www.forrester.com/press-newsroom/forrester-the-state-of-business-buying-2024), 4 December 2024. Analyst press release; sample size not stated in the release.
- [Gartner, 61% of B2B buyers prefer a rep-free buying experience](https://gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-06-25-gartner-sales-survey-finds-61-percent-of-b2b-buyers-prefer-a-rep-free-buying-experience), 25 June 2025. Survey of 632 B2B buyers, August to September 2024.
- [FTC, Policy Statement Regarding Advertising Substantiation](https://www.ftc.gov/node/52431), 23 November 1984. Primary US regulatory statement; still the reference standard.
- [FTC, FTC Announces Crackdown on Deceptive AI Claims and Schemes](https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2024/09/ftc-announces-crackdown-deceptive-ai-claims-schemes?os=f), 25 September 2024. Regulator press release; allegations, not all cases resolved at the time.
- [FCA, Cryptoasset financial promotions: marketing to UK consumers](https://www.fca.org.uk/firms/cryptoassets/marketing-uk-consumers/printable/print). Regulator guidance page; detailed rules are in PS23/6.
